title: In situ Hi-C Protocol
text:
Scaled master mixes






NoteMath audit — how every volume is calculated





Core formula (all standard mixes):
\[V_{total} = V_{per\_sample} \times N_{samples} \times 1.10\]
Formaldehyde crosslinking — working backwards from 1% final in ~10 mL/sample:
\[V_{16\%\;stock} = \frac{N_{cells} \times 1.1}{0.16} \; mL\]
Glycine quench — to reach 0.2M final from 2M stock:
\[V_{2M\;glycine} = \frac{N_{cells} \times 1.1}{10} \; mL\]
Biotin fill-in — ⚠️ 5% excess ONLY (not 10%):
\[V_{total} = V_{per\_sample} \times N_{samples} \times \mathbf{1.05}\]
Biotin-14-dATP costs ~$800/vial. The 5% exception is intentional and hardcoded.

fmt = (x, d = 1) => x.toFixed(d)
e   = n_samples * 1.10
e5  = n_samples * 1.05

title: In situ Hi-C Protocol
text:
Day 0 — Crosslinking






WarningFormaldehyde — fume hood only



All formaldehyde steps must be performed in a fume hood. Collect formaldehyde-exposed waste separately for disposal per institutional guidelines. Glycine quench must be added in the hood before moving tubes to bench.








TipCounting cells before crosslinking





Plate an extra well at the same density as your experimental wells and count from that well on Day 0. Do not count from your experimental wells — removing cells for counting changes the density of the remaining cells.

gl = (n_cells_M * 1.1 / 10).toFixed(2)

  {Step: "2", Action: `Add 1% formaldehyde (${fa} mL of 16% stock/sample); 10 min RT`,                     Detail: "Fume hood; rock gently"},
  {Step: "3", Action: `Quench: ${gl} mL 2M glycine/sample → 0.2M final; 5 min RT`,                         Detail: "Rock; RT"},

Day 1 — Lysis & MboI restriction digest (~2 hr + O/N)






WarningMboI handling



Keep MboI in the glycerol block on ice at all times. Return to –20°C immediately after dispensing. Never let it sit at room temperature — glycerol-containing enzymes lose activity quickly when warmed.








NoteWhy 0.5% SDS + Triton X-100 quench?





SDS permeabilizes nuclei to allow MboI access to chromatin. However, SDS also inhibits MboI, so it must be quenched with Triton X-100 before adding enzyme. The 62°C step ensures denaturation of surface proteins without denaturing chromatin structure.

title: In situ Hi-C Protocol
section: Day 2 — Biotin fill-in, ligation & crosslink reversal (~6.5 hr + O/N)
text:
Day 2 — Biotin fill-in, ligation & crosslink reversal (~6.5 hr + O/N)






Warning5% excess only for biotin fill-in — not 10%



Biotin-14-dATP is extremely expensive. The biotin fill-in master mix uses 5% excess (not the standard 10%). This is the only step in the protocol with a different excess factor.








NoteWhy proximity ligation at RT with slow rotation?





Proximity ligation must occur while chromatin is still condensed inside intact nuclei — this ensures only DNA ends that are spatially close get ligated. Elevated temperature or vigorous mixing would release chromatin and allow random intermolecular ligation, destroying the contact information.











Step
Action
Detail




1
Inactivate MboI: 62°C 20 min; cool to RT
Set oven to 23°C (open door)


2
Add 50 µL biotin fill-in mix — 5% excess only
37°C 1.5h rotation


3
Add 900 µL ligation mix; RT 4h slow rotation
Slowest oven speed; door open


4
Spin 2500×g 5 min; remove supernatant
—


5
Resuspend in 546 µL crosslink reversal mix; 55°C 30 min
Thermomixer


6
Continue 68°C O/N; no shaking
—

title: In situ Hi-C Protocol
text:
Day 4 — Shearing & size selection (~6.5 hr)






WarningTarget size is 300–500 bp — verify with gel before proceeding



If shearing is outside this range, the size selection will be off and library complexity will suffer. Run a 1:5 dilution on a 2% agarose gel before proceeding to AMPure. Do not skip the gel check.








TipAMPure size selection logic





The two-step AMPure protocol selects for 300–500 bp fragments. Step 1 (0.55×): large fragments (>500 bp) bind beads, small fragments (<500 bp) stay in supernatant — keep supernatant. Step 2 (add 0.15× more to supernatant): now 300–500 bp fragments bind — keep these beads. Fragments <300 bp remain in supernatant and are discarded.











Step
Action
Detail




1
Qubit BR; if >150 ng/µL dilute to 150 ng/µL in 130 µL
—


2
Covaris LE220: Duty 25 / PIP 500 / 200 cyc/burst / 90 sec
130 µL microTUBE; fill level 6


3
Transfer + wash vial with 70 µL ddH₂O → 200 µL total
—


4
Gel verify shearing: 1:5 dilution on 2% agarose
Use bottom layer of gel


5

<500 bp in supernatant


6
Add 0.15× more AMPure (30 µL) to supernatant; keep beads
300–500 bp on beads


7

—


8

Store –20°C

Day 1 — Cell binding to ConA beads (~2 hr)






NoteWhy ConA beads?





Concanavalin A-coated beads bind to the cell surface via glycoproteins, immobilizing cells for all subsequent washes. This eliminates centrifugation steps that would pellet and stress the nuclei. The key is that cells remain membrane-intact throughout — you are not isolating nuclei.

Day 2 — pAG-MNase & chromatin digestion (~4 hr)






WarningCaCl₂ addition triggers digestion immediately



Once CaCl₂ is added, MNase is active. Work quickly and consistently — keep all samples on ice until the moment you add CaCl₂ to each tube, then incubate exactly 30 min at 4°C. Longer digestion = smaller fragments = loss of signal at broad domains.










Step
Action
Detail




1
Pulse spin; magnet; wash Triton Buffer
1 mL/sample


2

Working solutions — scaled to sample count






NoteMath audit — how every volume is calculated





CitraHB Complete (10 mL aliquot per sample — used in Steps 2, 3, and 6):
\[V_{aliquot} = 10\;mL \times N_{samples} \times (1 + overage)\]
Additives (SUPERase, RNAsin, spermidine, spermine, DTT) scale linearly with \(V_{aliquot}\); protease inhibitor tablets are whole units, so the tablet count rounds up.
Iodixanol step gradient — each of the three working solutions is made by diluting 50% iodixanol (itself made 5 parts OptiPrep : 1 part Diluent, since OptiPrep ships at 60% and \(5/6 \times 60\% = 50\%\)) down to the target percentage with CitraPrepHB, using \(C_1V_1 = C_2V_2\):
\[V_{50\%\ stock\ needed} = V_{total} \times \frac{\%_{target}}{50\%} \qquad V_{diluent} = V_{total} - V_{50\%\ stock\ needed}\]
Per-sample total volumes (from the source calculation): 15 mL of 50% (kept as-is), 4 mL of 40%, and 7.5 mL of 30%. All three scale with \(N_{samples} \times (1+overage)\).
Polyamine additives in each gradient solution scale as \(V_{total}/1000\) (spermidine, spermine, DTT — 1000X). SUPERase and RNAsin scale as:
\[V_{stock} = \frac{C_{final}}{C_{stock}} \times V_{total}\]
This protocol targets \(C_{final} = 0.5\) U/µL for each inhibitor (not 0.2 U/µL), assuming a \(C_{stock} = 40\) U/µL stock — both are single-source-of-truth cells (rnase_final, rnase_stock) up top, so edit them there if your stock concentration differs.

Nuclei resuspension buffer (30 mL aliquot per sample):
\[V_{buffer} = 30\;mL \times N_{samples} \times (1+overage)\]
Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA) scales as 1% w/v of \(V_{buffer}\); SUPERase and RNAsin use the same \(C_{final}/C_{stock} \times V_{buffer}\) formula above. No spermine, spermidine, or Dithiothreitol (DTT) — these interfere with downstream cDNA synthesis.

TipHemocytometer counting method



CitraPrep nuclei yields are typically too low for a reliable Countess (automated) read, so this is a manual hemocytometer count every time — do not substitute the Countess.

Filter your trypan blue stock through a 0.2 µm filter before use — unfiltered trypan blue carries particulates that get miscounted as nuclei, and this matters more at low nuclei numbers where a few false counts skew the result.
Mix the nuclei suspension with filtered trypan blue at a 1:1 ratio (e.g. 10 µL suspension + 10 µL trypan blue) — dilution factor = 2.
Load 10 µL of the mix onto the hemocytometer; let it wick in by capillary action, no bubbles.
Under the microscope, count nuclei in the 4 corner grid squares (16 small squares each). Use the standard hemocytometer counting rule: count nuclei touching the top and left borders of a square, but not the bottom or right, to avoid double-counting nuclei that sit on a line.
Calculate concentration:

\[Nuclei/mL = \frac{\text{sum of nuclei in 4 corner squares}}{4} \times 2\ (\text{dilution factor}) \times 10^4\]
Divide by 1000 to convert to nuclei/µL for loading calculations.

10x Genomics ships this step as a large printed lookup table (Cell Stock Concentration × Targeted Cell Recovery, CG000731 p.34–35) rather than a formula. Back-calculating from >10 entries spanning both halves of that table gives a consistent relationship:

Step 3: 3’ Gene Expression Library Construction






NoteObjective



Enzymatic fragmentation and double-sided size selection optimize the cDNA amplicon size. P5 and P7 adaptors, i7 and i5 sample indexes, and a TruSeq Read 2 (read 2 primer sequence) are then added via End Repair, A-tailing, Adaptor Ligation, and PCR. The final libraries carry the P5 and P7 primers used for Illumina cluster generation and amplification.

Only 10 µL (25%) of the 40 µL total cDNA from Step 2.3m goes into fragmentation — regardless of total yield. Step 4: Sequencing






NoteObjective



A Chromium Single Cell 3’ Gene Expression Dual Index library is a standard Illumina paired-end construct beginning and ending with P5 and P7. The 16 bp 10x Barcode and 12 bp UMI are encoded in Read 1, while Read 2 sequences the cDNA fragment itself. i7 and i5 index sequences are read as separate sample index reads for demultiplexing. TruSeq Read 1 and TruSeq Read 2 are the standard Illumina sequencing primer sites used for paired-end sequencing.

WarningIndex hopping mitigation



Store each library individually (4°C ≤72 h, or −20°C long-term) — do not pool during storage. Pool only immediately before sequencing; an extra 1.0X SPRI cleanup on the pooled libraries can remove residual free adaptors. Never pool two libraries sharing the same sample index in one lane — this breaks demultiplexing.


Compatible sequencers: MiSeq, NextSeq 500/550/2000, HiSeq 2500 (Rapid Run), HiSeq 3000/4000, NovaSeq 6000. Data is analyzed with Cell Ranger (BCL/FASTQ → BAM, MEX, CSV, HDF5, web summary, .cloupe) and visualized in Loupe Browser.
